objective.objectiveLatex: Expand products of polynomials correctly, factor polynomials over the integers completely, and use a factorization to evaluate an expression at a convenient value.

prerequisites.noteLatex: Multiplying out a bracket is the distributive law, and the only prerequisite beyond [m1-l1](/M1/lessons/m1-l1) is comfort with negative numbers and with reading a coefficient as a multiplier rather than as a label.

concept.conceptLatex:
Multiplying polynomials is the distributive law applied more than once, and the only place a mistake can happen is bookkeeping: a term that fails to appear, a sign that flips unnoticed, or a coefficient that never gets combined. The rules are short, and they are cheaper to trust than to re-derive.

Start with monomials, because that fixes the vocabulary. Powers of the same base multiply by adding exponents, and coefficients multiply. A product in which different variables appear does not collapse into a single term: the exponent of each letter is tracked separately.

$3x^{2} \times 4x^{3} = 12x^{5} \qquad x^{2}y \times xy^{3} = x^{3}y^{4}$

Division reverses multiplication, so exponents subtract, and the inequality direction must reverse whenever the base being compared is negative.

$\frac{x^{7}}{x^{2}} = x^{5} \qquad \frac{6x^{4}y}{2x^{2}} = 3x^{2}y$

Distributing a monomial over a sum multiplies every term by it, and a term multiplied by zero vanishes, which is the usual reason a term goes missing from a result.

$3x(2x^{2}-5x+7) = 6x^{3}-15x^{2}+21x$

A binomial times a binomial produces four products that collapse into three terms. Multiply the first terms, the outer terms, the inner terms, and the last terms; the two middle ones are usually like terms and combine.

$(ax+b)(cx+d) = acx^{2} + (ad+bc)x + bd$

$(2x+3)(4x-1) = 8x^{2}-2x+12x-3 = 8x^{2}+10x-3$

The square of a binomial always has three terms, and the middle one carries a factor of $2$ that is never a matter of judgement.

$(a+b)^{2} = a^{2}+2ab+b^{2} \qquad (a-b)^{2} = a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}$

The difference of squares is the most useful single factorization in competition algebra, because it turns one subtraction into a product of two shorter expressions. The sum of two squares is the important exception: it does not factor over the integers.

$a^{2}-b^{2} = (a-b)(a+b) \qquad a^{2}+b^{2} \text{ does not factor over the integers}$

Cubes factor as well, and the sum of cubes is the mirror image of the difference of squares with the middle sign flipped.

$a^{3}-b^{3} = (a-b)(a^{2}+ab+b^{2}) \qquad a^{3}+b^{3} = (a+b)(a^{2}-ab+b^{2})$

Factoring reverses all of it. Take out the greatest common factor first, always, because it changes what is left over. Then test the remainder against a short list of structural patterns in a fixed order: difference of squares, perfect-square trinomial, then two integers whose sum and product are read off the coefficients.

$x^{2}-14x+49 = (x-7)^{2} \qquad x^{2}+5x+6 = (x+2)(x+3) \qquad x^{2}+2x-8 = (x+4)(x-2)$

When the leading coefficient is not $1$, either clear the common factor first or clear the denominators inside each factor.

$6x^{2}+11x+3 = (2x+1)(3x+3) = 3(2x+1)(x+1)$

Two habits prevent nearly every factoring error. Expand the result to confirm it reproduces the original. And read a factorization as a claim about signs: if the constant term is negative then exactly one of the factors has a negative constant, and if the constant term is positive then either both do or neither does.

There is a payoff that does not require factoring at all. If $P(x)$ is a polynomial, then $P(a)-P(b)$ is divisible by $a-b$, and when $P(a)=0$ the factorization makes $P(b)$ a product in which one factor is already known.

$P(x) = (x-2)(x+5) \implies P(-5) = 0$

Factorization is also not unique, and swapping the order of two factors changes nothing. A factorization is correct when it multiplies back to the original, not when it resembles the one expected.

examples.titleLatex: Worked example: a binomial times a binomial
examples.bodyLatex:
All four products, then combine the middle two.

$(2x+3)(4x-1) = 8x^{2}-2x+12x-3 = 8x^{2}+10x-3$

The middle coefficient is the sum $-2x+12x=10x$, which is the single most common place for a sign slip.

examples.titleLatex: Worked example: a perfect-square trinomial read backwards
examples.bodyLatex:
The last term is $49=7^{2}$ and the roots of the auxiliary quadratic $t^{2}-14t+49$ are both $7$, so the middle coefficient is forced.

$x^{2}-14x+49 = (x-7)^{2}$

The check is the expansion, which reproduces the middle term $-14x$ rather than the $+14x$ that a careless reading gives.

examples.titleLatex: Worked example: a leading coefficient that is not one
examples.bodyLatex:
The product of the outer coefficients is $18$, and the pairs adding to $11$ are $(-1)$ and $(-18)$ or $(-6)$ and $(-3)$.

$6x^{2}+11x+3 = (2x+1)(3x+3)$

Removing the content gives the complete factorization $3(2x+1)(x+1)$, and expanding it returns $6x^{2}+11x+3$.

Because $P$ is already factored, one factor is known to be zero, so no arithmetic is needed.

$P(x) = (x-2)(x+5) \implies P(-5) = (-7)(0) = 0$

Expanding first would give $x^{2}+3x-10$ and then $P(-5) = 25-15-10 = 0$, the same value by a longer road.

items.name: Add exponents when the base matches
items.summaryLatex: Multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents, and the coefficients multiply separately.
items.bodyLatex: Track each variable independently, since a product containing two different variables never collapses to one term. Division by a power of the same base subtracts the exponents.

items.name: Distribute to every term inside
items.summaryLatex: A multiplier outside a parenthesis acts on each term inside it, and a term multiplied by zero disappears.
items.bodyLatex: Counting the terms before and after the expansion catches a missing product immediately, because a distribution can never create or destroy a term.

items.name: Four products, three terms
items.summaryLatex: The product of two binomials has four cross-products, and the two middle ones combine into the linear term.
items.bodyLatex: Writing the general form $(ax+b)(cx+d)=acx^{2}+(ad+bc)x+bd$ makes the middle coefficient $ad+bc$ explicit rather than a matter of memory.

items.name: Square of a binomial
items.summaryLatex: $(a+b)^{2}=a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}$ and $(a-b)^{2}=a^{2}-2ab+b^{2}$, with the sign of the middle term following the sign between the two terms.
items.bodyLatex: A perfect-square trinomial must satisfy two independent conditions, on the first and last coefficients and on the middle one, and both are needed before factoring.

items.name: Take out the greatest common factor first
items.summaryLatex: Removing the content of the polynomial first is what exposes the structural pattern in what remains.
items.bodyLatex: The content is the greatest common divisor of all coefficients together with the largest common power of the variable. A negative content is usually taken as positive with one factor negated.

items.name: Difference of squares
items.summaryLatex: $a^{2}-b^{2}=(a-b)(a+b)$, which applies to any expression that is visibly a square minus a square.
items.bodyLatex: The sum of two squares has no such factorization over the integers, and a negative sign in front of the whole expression can be absorbed into one factor.

items.name: Sum and difference of cubes
items.bodyLatex: The middle term of the quadratic factor follows the same sign rule as the linear factor, which is a quick way to remember which of the two forms applies.

items.name: Use a factorization to evaluate
items.summaryLatex: When a polynomial is written as a product and one factor vanishes at the value being substituted, the whole value is zero.
items.bodyLatex: This turns an evaluation into a one-line observation and is the reason contest problems hand out a factored form in the first place.

items.titleLatex: Losing the middle term of a trinomial when squaring a binomial
items.whyLatex: The square of a binomial has three terms, and the middle term $2ab$ is the one a two-step mental shortcut drops. The correct expansion of $(x+5)^{2}$ is $x^{2}+10x+25$.
items.fixLatex: Write all three terms from the pattern before simplifying anything, and confirm the middle coefficient is twice the product of the two terms being squared.

items.titleLatex: Factoring a sum of two squares
items.whyLatex: The middle term of $(a+b)^{2}$ is $2ab$, so the expansion is $a^{2}+2ab+b^{2}$, not $a^{2}+b^{2}$. Over the integers $a^{2}+b^{2}$ does not factor at all.
items.fixLatex: Only a difference of squares factors that way. When the sign between the two squares is positive, look for a sum of cubes or a trinomial pattern instead.

items.titleLatex: Reporting a factorization that has not been multiplied back
items.whyLatex: The product on the right is $x^{2}+7x+6$, so the middle coefficient is wrong. The pairs that multiply to $6$ are $1$ and $6$, and $2$ and $3$, and only the second of those adds to $5$.
items.fixLatex: Multiply the factors back before reporting. For a trinomial the check is a sum and a product at once, so both conditions must hold simultaneously.
